content: Activities like TB infection control, while critical, have also been difficult to quantify. It is essential to monitor the entire continuum of care for individuals co-infected with HIV and TB, from screening and testing to treatment. This includes linking HIV-positive TB patients to both TB treatment and antiretroviral therapy (ART). To evaluate the quality of services, countries should also track loss to follow-up throughout the care cascade. Special considerations are necessary for certain populations at higher risk for HIV and TB or those requiring tailored service delivery. The World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), and UNAIDS have developed general guidelines for these populations. These include the Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Prevention, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Care for Key Populations and the Policy Guidelines for the Integrated Management of TB, HIV, and Viral Hepatitis in People Who Inject Drugs. Specific guidance on monitoring and evaluating TB services is outlined in the Technical Guide for Countries to Set Targets for Universal Access to HIV Prevention, Treatment, and Care. Measuring the risk of TB among healthcare workers compared to the general population is a recommended global and national indicator. The prevalence of active TB among people living with HIV who are newly enrolled in HIV care is a core indicator. Early detection of TB in this population enables timely TB treatment and early initiation of ART. This indicator indirectly reflects efforts to detect HIV-associated TB. Similarly, measuring HIV prevalence among registered TB patients helps guide resource allocation and monitor the effectiveness of HIV prevention interventions. High ART coverage among HIV-positive TB patients during TB treatment indicates strong collaboration between national HIV and TB programs. Monitoring the initiation of treatment for latent TB infection (LTBI) among people newly enrolled in HIV care is also critical, as LTBI treatment reduces the TB burden in this population. In many settings, data specific to key populations cannot be collected through routine program monitoring and require surveys. Additionally, assessing the timeliness of ART initiation after TB diagnosis is crucial, particularly for profoundly immunosuppressed HIV-positive TB patients. HIV-related comorbidities, including both infectious and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), are increasingly observed as more individuals receive ART and detection improves. In lowand middle-income settings, TB, severe bacterial infections, and other opportunistic infections (OIs) remain the leading causes of HIV-associated morbidity and mortality. In high-income countries, the pattern of comorbidities has shifted, with chronic liver disease, cardiovascular disease, and non-AIDS malignancies becoming more prominent. Certain cancers disproportionately affect people living with HIV, including Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and cervical cancer, which are classified as AIDS-defining malignancies. ART reduces the risk and improves survival for Kaposi sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma but does not lower the incidence of cervical cancer. The incidence of other cancers, such as Hodgkin lymphoma and anal cancer, has increased among HIV-infected individuals since the introduction of ART. Prevention, early diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of cancer in people living with HIV should adhere to clinical best practices. Mental health disorders, including depression, mania, cognitive disorders, and dementia, are common among people living with HIV. Certain antiretroviral drugs, like efavirenz, are linked to central nervous system side effects. HIV coinfection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a significant concern, with an estimated 5–25% of people living with HIV also having chronic HBV or HCV. Coinfection increases the severity of liver disease, the risk of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality, while reducing treatment response. Routine screening for HBV and HCV in ART programs is not yet standard, but WHO is developing guidelines to address this gap. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is now a cornerstone of national health sector responses to HIV. Monitoring ART scale-up is critical for tracking progress in the HIV prevention and treatment cascade. Recent WHO recommendations emphasize earlier initiation of ART, regardless of CD4 count, for certain groups, including children under five, pregnant women, and TB patients. Retention in HIV care is vital for improving patient outcomes and preventing the development of HIV drug resistance. Electronic patient monitoring systems can facilitate tracking and analysis of longitudinal patient outcomes, but challenges remain, particularly in decentralized settings. Unique patient identifiers and compatible electronic systems across facilities can help reduce data gaps and improve retention monitoring. In summary, comprehensive monitoring and evaluation of HIV and TB care, including ART retention, comorbidities, and coinfections, are essential for improving patient outcomes and guiding public health interventions.
